intro: Berlioz places an execution march inside a symphony, with a brief recollection of the beloved’s melody near its end. What happens to the regular tread when that recollection interrupts it?
question: How can a march turn a melody into an interruption?

sections.label: Minor-key return and build-up
sections.mNote: descending minor-key march returns, then gains orchestral weight

relations.label: The major-key march returns
relations.basis: The march’s second theme returns with a more active accompaniment, rather than an exposition restart; this agrees with the major-key march region in the listening notes and the structural account at https://human.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Music/Ethnomusicology/Resonances_-_Engaging_Music_in_its_Cultural_Context_(Morgan-Ellis_Ed.)/02%3A_Music_for_Storytelling/06%3A_Stories_without_Words/6.02%3A_Hector_Berlioz_-_Fantastical_Symphony. CENS diagonal mean 0.955, sustained 41 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 41.5 s (cache/form/berlioz-fantastique-march.txt, candidate 1; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: An execution in a dream
cues.text: This is the fourth of five movements. In Berlioz’s printed programme, an opium-dazed musician dreams that he has murdered his beloved and is being led to execution. Listen for the contrast between the march’s heavy tread and its more ceremonial passages.
cues.evidence: Berlioz’s published programme, part four, describes the dream and the march’s contrasting characters.

cues.title: A descending march tune
cues.text: The opening stretch builds around a descending tune in the low register. Follow the downward motion and its interruptions: a march can keep a regular tread without giving every phrase an uninterrupted line.
cues.evidence: The score places the descending tune after the introduction; an audio change near 0:18 gives only an approximate location.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The beloved as melody
cues.text: Berlioz’s programme calls the recurring melody an idée fixe: a persistent idea. It represents the beloved across all five movements, so the march belongs to a larger musical narrative rather than an independent military scene.
cues.evidence: The 1845 programme’s first movement explains the recurring melodic image and its connection to the beloved.

cues.title: A more ceremonial march
cues.text: Around this part of the march, the sound grows stronger and more brilliant. Compare the broad tune with the earlier descending line, while keeping track of the tread beneath it.
cues.evidence: The measured relative level rises by about 18 dB from 1:30 to 1:40, with more energy in the upper frequencies.

cues.title: Paris hears the symphony
cues.text: François-Antoine Habeneck conducted the premiere at the Paris Conservatoire on 5 December 1830. Berlioz later recalled the march’s strong reception, while admitting that two rehearsals had not been enough for a flawless performance.
cues.evidence: Berlioz’s Memoirs, chapter 31, describes the premiere, its rehearsals and the march’s reception.

cues.title: Withdrawal and renewed force
cues.text: This stretch contains a pronounced withdrawal followed by another build-up. Follow how the march keeps its forward motion through the change in level, rather than treating the quieter passage as a new tempo.
cues.evidence: Relative level falls sharply around 2:50 and rises again across the following 20 seconds.

cues.title: One night, later revisions
cues.text: In his memoirs Berlioz says he wrote the march in one night. In the same account he says that he continued altering it, and the other movements, over several years; speed of first composition did not mean a finished score.
cues.evidence: Berlioz makes both statements in Memoirs, chapter 26; they are his retrospective account.

cues.title: A thought before the blow
cues.text: Near the close, the march makes room for a brief recollection before the final outburst. Berlioz’s programme describes this as a last thought of love, interrupted by the execution; listen for the scale of the contrast rather than a complete restatement of the melody.
cues.evidence: The programme identifies the recollection; a marked fall in relative level around 4:12 supports its approximate position, not a clarinet entrance.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The closing outburst
cues.text: The final stretch sets a short, quiet recollection against a much stronger ending. In the programme, the interruption is fatal: the major-key close does not mean a reprieve for the condemned musician.
cues.evidence: The score and programme establish the ending; the relative level rises by about 21 dB between 4:20 and 4:25.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: One movement still remains
cues.text: The march’s closing chords are not the end of the symphony. A fifth movement follows: the dream of a witches’ sabbath, where Berlioz’s programme describes the beloved’s melody transformed into a grotesque dance.
cues.evidence: Berlioz’s published programme gives the fifth movement this scene and describes the melody’s transformation.

transitions.title: The bass acquires a marching line
transitions.how: The introduction establishes G minor through low orchestral weight and timpani rather than a complete tune. Cellos and double basses turn that preparation into the descending march melody: the bass is now the subject, not merely its support. The regular duple tread survives the hand-over, while orchestral replies break up the low line. Listen for continuity of pulse beneath the change from repeated, expectant sounds to a directed descent.
transitions.evidence: The section boundary is 0:18, also the report’s strongest novelty peak; relative level rises across 0:15–0:25. The written introduction and low-string descending theme supply the instrumental and G-minor description; the report does not identify individual entrances.

transitions.title: The procession changes its public face
transitions.how: The descending G-minor material gives way to the broad march in B♭ major, its relative major. Berlioz changes the foreground from low strings to a wind-and-brass-led tune, with sharply articulated accompaniment underneath. The preceding withdrawal makes the new orchestral weight register as an arrival; it does not require a new marching speed. The join contrasts minor and major, low melodic register and projected upper melody, while preserving the same two-beat gait.
transitions.evidence: The Brass-led march boundary at 1:38 coincides with a novelty peak. Relative level rises from −30.4 dB at 1:30 to −12.3 dB at 1:40 and brightness increases. The score supplies the B♭-major second march; the relations file identifies its later varied repetition, not an exposition restart.

transitions.title: The low march takes control again
transitions.how: After the major-key march and its more active repetition, Berlioz withdraws the ceremonial weight and restores G minor. The descending material again gives the lower register a leading role, then becomes fuel for a renewed orchestral build-up. The join works by subtraction before accumulation: the tread continues, but the texture contracts so that the returning minor-key line can be heard before brass and percussion enlarge it.
transitions.evidence: The section boundary is 2:50; the report shows a novelty peak and a fall from −8.3 dB at 2:45 to −21.4 dB at 2:50, followed by a rise towards 3:10. The minor-key return and renewed treatment of the descending theme are score-derived; the measured recurrence excerpts are not exact section limits.

transitions.title: A solo voice interrupts the crowd
transitions.how: Berlioz cuts back the massed march to expose the clarinet’s fragment of the idée fixe. This is not a transition made by developing the march tune: a melody from the symphony’s first movement interrupts it. G major replaces the prevailing minor, and a sustained, singing line displaces the clipped collective tread. The thinning of bass and accompaniment makes the remembered phrase sound precariously unsupported; it is allowed no complete melodic or cadential conclusion.
transitions.evidence: The Last recollection boundary is 4:12, a strong novelty peak; relative level drops from −9.0 dB at 4:10 to −28.3 dB at 4:15. The score and Berlioz’s programme establish the solo clarinet quotation and its interruption. The timestamp locates the passage, not the clarinet’s first note.

transitions.title: The cadence is taken by force
transitions.how: The clarinet does not finish its sentence. A full-orchestra blow cuts across it, followed by a brief pizzicato gesture and the emphatic G-major close. Berlioz replaces melodic continuation with an attack, then with repeated chordal confirmation: brass, percussion and the orchestral bass leave no room for the solo line to resume. The major tonic is the crowd’s conclusion, not a resolution of the interrupted love melody.
transitions.evidence: The Execution and close boundary is 4:24; nearby novelty peaks occur at 4:20 and 4:24, and relative level rises by about 21 dB between 4:20 and 4:25. The orchestral interruption, pizzicato gesture and G-major ending are written events; no individual attack is claimed to be aligned.

facts: Flute and guitar as a boy; Paris Conservatoire with Jean-François Le Sueur and Anton Reicha
Critic for the Journal des débats; Conservatoire librarian; touring conductor
Shakespeare, Goethe and Virgil supplied the subjects of his largest works
Four symphonies; operas; dramatic and sacred choral works; songs; an orchestration treatise
composer.background:
Berlioz grew up in La Côte-Saint-André, between Lyon and Grenoble, in the household of a physician who taught him Latin and expected him to study medicine. He learned flute and guitar, but never acquired the pianist’s routine of composing at a keyboard. Virgil’s account of Dido’s death affected him as a schoolboy; forty years later he would set it in Les Troyens. Sent to Paris in 1821, he attended anatomy lectures while spending his evenings at the Opéra. The theatre’s performances of Gluck offered a different education: declamation, orchestral gesture and the pacing of a dramatic scene.

He abandoned medicine, studied with Jean-François Le Sueur and entered the Conservatoire in 1826. His first large works included a Messe solennelle and the unfinished opera Les Francs-juges, whose overture survived independently. The Prix de Rome required a prescribed cantata; Berlioz finally won it in 1830, on his fourth attempt. The prize sent him to the Villa Medici, but the decisive musical experiences had already happened in Paris. Conservatoire performances under François-Antoine Habeneck introduced him to Beethoven’s symphonies, while an English theatrical company introduced him to Shakespeare.
composer.epithet: He made orchestral colour, the position of a sound in space, and the return of a remembered melody into structural events.
